#4420. Digital Detox: The Return of the Knobs, and Those Who Obsess Over Them

The Aughts were an amazing time for automobiles. Tactile switchgear, in retrospect, was part of it.

My most enduring professional memories of the Aughts are as follows: (1) Driving a Porsche Carrera GT with Walter Röhrl. (2) Being constantly harangued by German auto engineers about the absolute superiority of diesel engines. (3) Hyperextending my neck while driving the Grave Digger monster truck. And (4) listening to Audi rhapsodize about its obsession with the quality and feel of its switchgear.

This story originally appeared in Volume 38 of Road & Track.

With two decades’ distance from that time, here is my assessment of the above: (1) Sick! Peak experience. Could have probably just stopped after this and been satisfied. (2) The German auto engineers were wrong, although it took a gargantuan scandal, the expenditure of many fortunes, and the threat of a diesel-powered Audi R8 for the evangelists to finally accept the truth. (3) That hurt a lot, but I also ripped the door off the truck on a landing, so call it even. (4) I might have scoffed at Audi’s fixation at the time, but in the touchscreen world we now live in, I miss those switches and knobs. So much so, in fact, that I would happily hear again about the company’s knob-research department.

And so, as I stood out in the California sunshine on a recent day, listening to the Audi CEO, Gernot Döllner, positively geek out over the switchgear and beautifully designed accoutrements of the company’s new Nuvolari supercar, it was a most comforting flashback. Seriously, the man clearly relished dragging a fingernail over the aluminum air vents inside the car and listening to them ring. The lever to adjust the vent is a fully realized and glorious device. Yes, I do understand how ­ridiculous that statement sounds. But this is an exquisitely rendered piece of aluminum operating so smoothly and consistently that your brain assumes you are in the presence of quality. You can’t help it. It’s biology! Inside and out, the car is peppered with these small, beautiful delights.

And yes, the Nuvolari is almost entirely a Lamborghini Temerario under its spare, Bauhausian skin. And yes, the limited-edition Nuvolari costs over $300,000 more than the Lambo, which, to a sensible human, makes no sense. But it is a marvelous thing to behold and touch. It’s a statement of intent from Audi to return the company’s focus to design and quality in general (as well as in switchgear and trimmings specifically). Let the rhapsodizing begin again. I’m here for it. Again.

Please enjoy this issue’s look into the Aughts, a decade that fundamentally changed cars and the culture around them. And check out the site for additional Aughts-worthy content, including a forthcoming comparison test of two V-12 ultraluxury sedans. Remember sedans?

#4419. West Coast Customs turns a Tesla Model 3 into a 1955 Chevy Bel Air

West Coast Customs has finished its first electric Chevy Bel Air, and there’s not much Chevy left under the paint. The Burbank shop cut the body off a Tesla Model 3, kept the entire rolling platform, and set a 1955 Bel Air shell on top of it.

The result, called Project B-Zero, looks like a ’55 Chevy from the curb and like a Model 3 as soon as you open the door. And it charges at Tesla Superchargers.

In the shop’s new video, “The First Ever Electric Bel Air,” founder and CEO Ryan Friedlinghaus explains that a longtime client, Troy Swope, wants to convert an entire car collection to electric and picked the Bel Air to go first. WCC had previously built the same client a Chevelle with a big gas engine.

Friedlinghaus, who drives a Tesla himself, decided against pulling the Model 3’s motors and battery out and fitting them into the old Chevy. Instead, the Tesla stays whole and the Chevy becomes the body kit.

That’s a formula WCC has used for years with gas cars. The shop calls it “old school meets new school”: an old GTO body on a new GTO, an old Camaro on a new Camaro, an old Mustang on a new Mustang. B-Zero is the first time it did it with a Tesla underneath.

“It sounds easy, but that process was tedious,” Friedlinghaus said.

Before any Chevy sheet metal went on, the crew took the bare Model 3 skateboard for a spin on the streets around the shop, with no doors, no lights and no seatbelts. Friedlinghaus joked about how many safety violations they were racking up. But it drove fine.

The real headache was the wheelbase. A 1955 Chevy rides on a 115-inch wheelbase, while the Model 3 sits at 113.2 inches. On its gas builds, WCC can cut, shorten or lengthen the newer car’s frame to match the old body. You can’t do that with a Tesla, since the floor is the battery pack.

So the shop changed the body instead, stretching the Bel Air’s rear wheel wells so the wheels sit where they look like they belong.

The client wanted the exterior to read as a mostly stock Bel Air. The original car was red, so WCC kept it red, with a satin finish and gloss black accents.

Inside, it’s a Model 3. The shop kept the Tesla’s interior, including the steering wheel and center touchscreen, and modified it to fit the Chevy body. The seats got black suede with white stitching in an octagon pattern that Friedlinghaus said was borrowed from the Lamborghini Urus, plus red accents and a “B-Zero” script on the dash.

Friedlinghaus said the goal was for people to see “a really nice Bel Air” from the outside, then open the door and find a Tesla. He also expects some double takes when it pulls into a Supercharger station.

He admits the reaction has been split. Plenty of people are mad that the shop electrified a Bel Air, and plenty of others think it came out great. The client is clearly in the second camp, describing the car as easy to drive and saying every trip in it feels like an event.

Here’s the full build video from West Coast Customs:

This is sick. I know Tesla doesn’t care about personal car ownership anymore, but they should really sell their platform so shops can do these conversions without using salvage vehicles.

Well I was really interested in this build until I read how they kept it entirely Tesla inside. Not at all what I was thinking or what I'd call a true old car conversion to EV. Instead, they simply transformed the outside of a Tesla into an old looking car. To me, even the outside looks too far removed from the original Bel Air and more like a street rod. If that's what the owner wants and paid for, great.

But for me, I would never do a conversion like that. I really want to convert an older 70's or 80's or early 90's Cadillac into an EV. But for me, I will insist that the outside and inside look 100% like the original car with just an EV powertrain.

Don’t get me wrong, if you can recycle a salvage, that’s good, but it can’t always be done.

Compare it to the 1966 Mustang that a Sacramento Tesla parts shop converted earlier this year. That project took about $40,000 and two years, with the team grafting sections of a Model 3 floor into the Mustang. It’s an amazing build, but it’s a lot of custom engineering. WCC’s approach skips most of that. You keep Tesla’s crash structure, battery thermal management, software, over-the-air updates and Supercharger access, because you never took the car apart in the first place. It’s closer to what S-Klub did with its Model 3-based Mercedes 300SL than a traditional drivetrain swap.

The purists will hate it. That’s fine. This Bel Air will get driven more in a year than most restored ones get driven in a decade.

#4418. The EV Charging Company That’s Quietly Conquering America Is Building A New U.S. Factory

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Alpitronic, the company that makes the DC fast chargers used by Ionna, Walmart, Mercedes-Benz, BP Pulse, and others, is building a new factory in the United States that will boost output of its 400- and 1,000-kilowatt stalls.

The manufacturer’s new 173,315-square-foot facility, located in Fort Mill, South Carolina, will create 70 new jobs and will also act as a testing lab, repair center, logistics hub, and warehouse.

Alpitronic, which has its North American headquarters in Charlotte, North Carolina, and its global headquarters in Bolzano, Italy, said it will invest $33.94 million in the new facility, with $200,000 coming from York County’s Coordinating Council for Economic Development in the form of a Set-Aside grant to assist with the costs of building improvements.

“North America is central to our next phase of growth, and investing in our manufacturing capabilities is key to supporting that expansion,” said Patrik Herrnegger, Alpitronic Americas CEO. “Our Fort Mill facility will put U.S. production under our direct control, bringing us closer to our customers and enabling us to serve them more efficiently. We thank South Carolina and York County for their partnership as we prepare to begin production in early 2027.”

Back in 2024, the company worked with a third-party production partner to open its first local manufacturing facility in Wisconsin. Now, manufacturing has moved in-house, with Alpitronic wholly owning the production operation.

The new South Carolina plant will assemble HYC400 and HYC1000 stalls, Alpitronic said. The HYC400 all-in-one dispensers can deliver up to 400 kW of power to a single connected electric vehicle without needing a separate power cabinet, and are the current charger of choice for Ionna and Walmart.

The higher-powered HYC1000 system is composed of a 1,000-kW power cabinet and up to four stalls that can deliver up to 600 kW to a single EV. Each stall can have two ports, and the system can dynamically allocate power to each vehicle to make the best use of the available power.

What makes the company's dispensers different from most competitors is the use of silicon carbide components, which lower energy losses and, subsequently, the amount of money EV drivers have to pay for a top-up. According to Alpitronic, SiC modules enable 97.5% efficiency and allow for smaller, quieter, and cooler stalls.

Alpitronic’s new factory in Fort Mill, South Carolina, is scheduled to go online in February 2027.

#4417. Never Before in the History of Motoring: How the Splendor and Madness Of the Aughts Shaped Today’s Car World

From the Ford GT to the Toyota Prius, from the birth of Tesla to the death of Pontiac, that decade turned the industry upside-down.

It was a perfect moment. In the driver’s seat of a 2005 Ford GT, with my best pal riding shotgun, I stared through the windshield with eyes opened as wide as the car’s headlights. The year was 2007. We were on a stretch of I-80 that dives down the eastern slopes of the Sierra Nevada mountains, from California into Nevada. The early-­morning sun hung low on the horizon in front of us. Looking out on the desert, we saw miles of empty highway, with visibility so sharp that we would see any highway patrol vehicle in our path.

This story originally appeared in Volume 38 of Road & Track.

It felt like driving a Michigan-made Millennium Falcon. This Ford could hit 200 mph and beat the Ferrari Challenge Stradale around a road course. It was shamelessly retro, trading hard on the Le Mans pedigree of its GT40 ancestor, but it was also new age and American as all hell. It felt unprecedented.

Looking back now, almost 20 years later, I can see that the word unprecedented applied to the whole decade. The Aughts, defined as the years 2000 to 2009, were packed with never-before events and spectacular vehicles such as the Ford GT. It was a time of excitement and optimism, when cars were cool and quicker than ever—until it all crashed into a ditch with the economic downturn. The era was to the car industry what the Sixties were to music, politics, and assassinations. An era of profound change. Of tremendous upheaval. Of darkness and light. Of death and rebirth.

It was the decade that shaped our here and now.

On the most macro level, the Aughts were when the global automotive ecosphere began ­reordering itself into what we know today. In 2008, ­Toyota overtook GM to become the world’s largest automaker, selling 8.97 million vehicles around the world that year. The ­DaimlerChrysler partner­ship shattered. General Motors, one of the largest corporations on earth, and Chrysler, another of Detroit’s Big Three, went bankrupt at the end of the decade, and if not for the federal government handing out bags of cash to bail out those legendary companies, they might no longer exist.

GM’s Oldsmobile and Pontiac, two brands that collectively had made cars for nearly 200 years, disappeared during the Aughts. (To be fair, Pontiac did make it a few days into the new decade, ending production on January 4, 2010, with a last-gasp G6 sedan.) Plymouth also went bye-bye. Saturn assembled its final vehicle in 2009.

The Aughts were also the start of credible alternatives to internal-combustion motoring’s hegemony. The Toyota Prius arrived in the United States in July 2000, then became a cultural lightning rod when sales of the second-­generation model exploded in response to surging gas prices. Hybrid, a term that often applied to a kind of cannabis at the time, suddenly became lingo referring to a kind of car. At the same time, there were inklings of a lithium-ion automotive future. Tesla put out its first battery-powered car, the Roadster, in 2008, and early adopters felt the shock of a 0–60 thrust without the jolt of gears changing. Cars began to morph from machinery into the rolling computer devices that we drive today, as screens proliferated on dashboards and our phones learned to talk to our vehicles. Digital technology wormed its way deeper into every aspect of motoring, a trend that continues, albeit with far less idealism now.

The decade was a history-defining time in motorsport as well. Globally, racing saw the dawn of a new dynastic epoch. Michael Schumacher, driving for Ferrari, claimed the Formula 1 world championship from 2000 to 2005. In large part, F1 has been a series defined by dynasties ever since. Audi and Tom Kristensen ruled Le Mans for nearly the entire decade, and for the first time, a turbo­diesel won: the R10 in 2006. In NASCAR, Jimmie Johnson took the Cup Series title five years in a row with Chevrolet starting in 2006.

Dynasties on this level of dominance had never happened before in any of these series. I remember sitting in a press conference after the Italian Grand Prix in 2006, when Schumacher (having just won the race) announced his first retirement. The moment he unleashed the news, he teared up and an explosion of camera flashes came from the press corps. The feeling in the room was unforgettable. What Schumacher had done during his career to that point was unprecedented.

Even pop culture had an auto­motive renaissance. The Fast and the Furious premiered on June 18, 2001, with three sequels in multiplexes before the decade was over. F&F grew into Universal Studios’ biggest film franchise and remains the most successful car-movie series ever. Pixar’s Cars came out in 2006 and became Paul Newman’s highest-grossing film, even though viewers never saw his face. Talladega Nights (also 2006) may not invite many critical superlatives, but it unapologetically roasted NASCAR, which was in on the joke. It also popularized the saying, “If you ain’t first, you’re last.” Michael Bay’s Transformers films filled theaters. There was even a Dukes of Hazzard movie with Jessica Simpson playing Daisy Duke, Burt Reynolds as Boss Hogg, and a badass General Lee Dodge Charger. Car video games saw surging popularity, sales, and advancements in graphics. The Aughts gave us Forza Motorsport, plus new and series-defining installments of Gran Turismo and Grand Theft Auto.

So much was happening in the car world that being a fan felt electrifying. The Camaro, the Charger, and the Challenger were back, and the Mustang was reborn in retro style. The first Cars & Coffee events happened in Southern California, and soon small towns around the U.S. were hosting them.

When you throw all of this together, it made for an earth-shattering decade. Despite the dizzying news cycle, however, it was the cars themselves that we remember most. The Aughts ushered in a new era for halo cars, when automakers set out to build masterpieces that created new expectations for performance and technology. Some would say the Seventies, Eighties, and Nineties were halcyon days for car fans. But the new sheetmetal that graced our roads in the first decade of the new millennium was incomparable.

Ford came up with the aforementioned GT, which was the first real Ford customer supercar made in any significant numbers. Porsche gave us the Carrera GT, a mid-engine rocket ship that is one of the greatest sports cars of all time. Bugatti chased even bigger numbers with the Veyron, the first road car that could crack 250 mph and produce 1000 hp.

There were plenty of other highlights as soaring corporate confidence and unheard-of development budgets ushered in the arrival of still more icons. This was the decade of the C6 Corvette Z06 and ZR1, the Audi R8, the Ferrari Enzo, and the Mercedes-Benz SLR McLaren. The Bentley Continental GT and the Porsche 911 GT3 RS debuted, along with the U.S.-eligible Nissan GT-R. V-8 engines were squeezed into the BMW M3, the Cadillac CTS-V, and the Mercedes-Benz C63 AMG. It was a time of heroes.

These cars didn’t just thrill us; they were so unique and outstanding that they redefined the identities of the brands that made them and even motoring itself. That is the true legacy of the Aughts. Even if you’re too young to have lived through those years, you are reaping the rewards today. Because of all of that innovation and ambition, the future through our windshields still looks bright. But maybe a little less bright than it did back then.

A.J. Baime is the author of seven books, including Go Like Hell: Ford, Ferrari, and Their Battle for Speed and Glory at Le Mans, and The Accidental President: Harry S. Truman and the Four Months that Changed the World. An R&T editor-at-large, he has driven cars on racetracks all over the U.S. and Europe, going back to 2007. He is proudly the R&T staff’s slowest track driver.

#4416. Rivian’s ALSO pauses high-tech e-bike deliveries over ‘software issues’ that we saw coming

Rivian’s new electric bike spinoff, ALSO, has hit another speed bump. The company has announced that it is temporarily halting deliveries of its TM-B electric bicycles after discovering software-related problems affecting some bikes, including issues with charging behavior.

And unfortunately, this isn’t entirely surprising. We’ve already reported on some strange battery behavior with the new e-bikes, as well as customers having to send their bikes back for repairs.

In a message sent to customers, ALSO explained that it was pausing shipments to address several software problems before more bikes reach riders.

“We’ve identified a few software-based issues, such as charging behavior, that are impacting some bikes,” the company explained.

ALSO says its engineers are working on a firmware update to resolve the problems, with shipments expected to resume in approximately two weeks.

The pause affects the remaining Launch Edition deliveries as well as the beginning of Performance Edition shipments, both of which will now arrive later than previously promised.

The announcement follows earlier reports of unusual charging and discharging behavior on the TM-B, which we previously highlighted as some of the growing pains facing Rivian’s ambitious new e-bike venture.

We’ve also reported on customers needing to return their bikes for repairs, raising questions about how smoothly the company’s initial rollout was progressing.

The issues align with many of our initial concerns we discussed a year ago when the bike was first unveiled, namely that the high-tech design means the bike incorporates many new and proprietary systems that could each lead to complicated and costly failures.

Now ALSO has officially acknowledged software problems affecting some bikes, including charging behavior, though it hasn’t detailed the full extent of the issues or confirmed whether they are directly related to those earlier reports.

I love the PR spin how only "some" bikes are affected. If it's the same bike running the same software, it's affected. The only bikes not affected are the ones that haven't been delivered, because they are not being used.

The bike represents a fairly radical departure from traditional electric bicycles, with proprietary technology throughout its drivetrain and control systems. That makes software an especially important part of the ownership experience.

To ALSO’s credit, pausing deliveries to fix known problems is probably the right move. Nobody wants to receive a premium-priced electric bicycle only to discover that it needs an immediate trip back to the manufacturer.

But for customers who have already waited longer than expected, another delay is undoubtedly frustrating.

ALSO says it will provide another update on November 24, hopefully with better news about when deliveries can resume.

#4415. Taking a Little off the Top: 1991 Saab 900S Test

From the August 1991 issue of Car and Driver.

Our friend Max has his heart set on a Saab. His brother Pete has a Saab with more than 100,000 miles on it, and Max swears the thing is still as tight as one of Madonna’s bustiers. Max also says—having read the brochures—that all Saabs now come with more standard equipment than a fire truck. “Seems to me,” says Max, “that no other car gives you as much quality and stuff for the money.”

Take the Swedish maker’s new-for-1991 900S convertible. You’ll note the absence of the word “Turbo” in that moniker. Previously, Saab’s only ragtop was the sprightly turbocharged edition—as nice a convertible as you’ll find, to be sure, but currently saddled with a $33,712 stick­er. Oh, and that price busts the $30K luxu­ry-tax barrier, so remember to add another $371 to the bottom line for Uncle Sam.

The new 900S convertible is the “affordable” Saab droptop; it lists for $28,712, no sin tax necessary. Of course, you have to give up something to save $5000-plus. That something is performance. Rather than the Turbo’s 160-horsepow­er 2.0-liter four, the 900S uses a new nor­mally aspirated, twin-cam, sixteen-valve 2.1-liter four-banger that produces 140 horsepower at 6000 rpm and 133 pound­-feet of torque at 2900. (For ’91, this engine is standard in all non-turbo 900 models.) Performance with this powerplant is modest—a run to 60 mph takes 9.6 sec­onds—but that doesn't seem to bother Max. “Hey,” he says, “not everybody wants to be Ayrton Senna.” In its favor, the engine revs smoothly, with a characteristic Saab whine, and delivers good fuel economy. Our test car turned in a 24-mpg average.

See all results for used cars for sale near 21014

The rest of the car is a near copy of the Turbo convertible. Which is to say, the 900S is one of the most satisfying sun cars around. The cloth top is power-operated; lowering it is as easy as unlocking two headliner latches and pushing a console­mounted button. With the top down, the body is tight and all but shake-free. Saab attributes the body’s rigidity to its pedigree: the droptop 900S is not a beheaded coupe but a designed-from-the-ground-up soft-top built on a dedicated production line.

As Max has rightly discovered, Saabs justify their sticker prices by being very well equipped. Included in the convertible’s $28,712 base price is everything a discern­ing driver is likely to want: a driver-side air bag; anti-lock brakes; leather seats; power windows, locks, and mirrors; a potent AM/FM/cassette stereo; fog lights; and a headlight wiper/washer system.

If the Saab’s price seems steep com­pared with such convertibles as the Chrysler LeBaron, the Olds Cutlass Supreme, or even the Mazda Miata, bear in mind that few buyers considering the Saab are likely to have those cars on their potential-purchases list. The 900S’s real competitors are such prestige sunsters as the BMW 325i, the Infiniti M30, and even the Cadillac Allanté. The 900S sells for substantially less than all of those, yet it’s on par in terms of refinement, luxury, solidity, and cachet.

See all results for used cars for sale near 21014

For once, it seems Max has made a decision we can’t argue with.

#4414. Rivian’s Also Spinoff Pauses Deliveries Of Its $3,500 E-Bike After Months Of Delays

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Also, the electric mobility startup spun off from Rivian, is facing another logistics headache. After delaying deliveries of its futuristic TM-B e-bike, the startup has paused shipments entirely to address some software problems that may lead to problematic charging behavior and phantom battery drain.

In an email sent to reservation holders, the company apologized for the delay, saying it has identified a few software-based issues that are impacting some bikes, and that it wants to address the issues before resuming shipments, as first reported by The Verge. A firmware update is in the works, and Also estimates that deliveries will resume in approximately two weeks, with another update scheduled for November 24.

This is the latest setback for the mobility spinoff that made headlines last year with its software-heavy bicycles and four-wheeled quads. The TM-B e-bike was originally scheduled to be shipped in the spring of this year, but customers started receiving their orders months later, leading to a barrage of negative comments on the Also subreddit. This prompted Saul Leiken, the startup’s product manager, to post a 661-word apology letter, in which he attributed the setbacks to strict quality standards and “significant supply chain challenges.”

An Also e-bike customer who received his e-bike posted a YouTube video showing how the TM-B behaves when the state of charge gets low, and how the battery drains while the bike is not in use. Aaron Draczyski said he charged his bike in the garage up to 70%, but the state of charge went down to 30% in 24 hours without any usage. What’s more, when the battery level became critically low, the bike refused to charge, throwing an error message that claimed the battery was not installed, even though it hadn’t been removed.

The Also TM-B is unlike most e-bikes out there. Designed from the ground up as a futuristic mobility vehicle, its pedals are not physically connected to the rear wheels. Instead, the rider spins a generator, which provides power to the battery and the electric motor that turns the rear wheel via a rubber belt.

The battery can be recharged via a USB-C port, there’s a round touchscreen to control all of the bike’s features, and the rider can also use a smartphone app to keep tabs on the bike remotely.

The base Also TM-B starts at $3,500, but the Launch Edition models, which have yet to be shipped, cost $4,500. Earlier this year, when the startup announced the first delays, it threw in one of its Alpha Wave helmets and a $250 credit to spend on accessories.

#4413. Tesla toughens FSD driver monitoring in Europe while loosening it in the US

Tesla is rolling out stricter driver monitoring for its “Full Self-Driving” system in Europe, with earlier warnings, a full strike for drivers who look away during a manoeuvre, and a hands-on-wheel requirement above 130 km/h (81 mph).

In the US, Tesla has spent the last year going the other way. Its CEO told owners they can text and drive on FSD, and recent US builds were tuned to nag drivers less.

On November 16, the Dutch vehicle authority RDW announced that it signed off on a new update to Tesla Assisted Driving, the name Tesla now uses for FSD (Supervised) in Europe. It covers HW4 vehicles and goes out over the air.

According to the RDW, drivers now get attention warnings earlier. If a driver isn’t paying attention while the system performs a manoeuvre, they get a “full strike.” The regulator says the update also adds measures to prevent misuse of the system, but it didn’t spell out what they are.

There’s a speed component too. Above 130 km/h (where legal), the driver has to keep their hands on the wheel. And setting a maximum speed above what the system displays now requires the driver to confirm it by scrolling the wheel up, with the speed limit sign pulsing red when the car goes over.

The RDW says it tested the update on its own track and on public roads and found no adverse or unintended effects. Ten other countries have adopted the Dutch approval so far, with Finland now on the list, while EU-wide approval is still waiting on a vote at the TCMV, the committee of member states.

This comes two weeks after Tesla cut the system’s speed margin from 50% to 10% over the limit in Europe and dropped the “Full Self-Driving” name there. Germany had made both a condition of supporting EU approval.

Now look at how Tesla handles the same software at home.

At Tesla’s shareholder meeting last November, Musk complained that the car was “a little strict about keeping your eyes on the road” and said Tesla would “allow you to text and drive essentially” within a month or two. A month later, an owner asked whether FSD v14.2.1 allowed texting. Musk’s answer: “Depending on context of surrounding traffic, yes.”

Texting while driving is illegal in 49 states. FSD is still a Level 2 system, and Tesla’s own fine print says the driver is responsible at all times.

In May, Musk confirmed that FSD v14.3.3 was built to nag drivers less. Tesla did add better eye-gaze tracking and eyewear handling in a June build, to be fair. But the pitch to owners hasn’t changed: fewer nags is sold as a feature.

And US drivers have been allowed to go hands-free on FSD at any speed since Tesla moved to cabin-camera monitoring in 2024. There’s no 130 km/h rule here.

NHTSA noticed. In its engineering analysis of FSD crashes in low-visibility conditions, the agency asked Tesla to justify a list of its marketing claims, and it specifically cited Musk’s texting post. In September, Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi asked NHTSA to look into Tesla’s driver monitoring after dozens of videos appeared to show drivers asleep on Autopilot and FSD.

The results are on the road. Last month, a driver told the CHP he was asleep on FSD when his Tesla drove through a freeway closure and hit a patrol car, seriously injuring two officers. Owners are also filming themselves defeating Tesla’s driver monitoring and posting it for clout.

Both markets get the same cabin camera and the same HW4 computer.

But in Europe, a type-approval authority tests every update before it ships and can refuse it. In the US, nobody pre-approves driver-assist software. Tesla self-certifies, and NHTSA only steps in after complaints and crashes pile up, which is how you end up with a CEO publicly telling owners to text while the regulator is still writing letters about it.

This update proves Tesla can build stricter driver monitoring whenever a regulator demands it. The code exists. It’s running on HW4 cars in 11 European countries right now.

That's because Musk is buddies with the current federal government that would regulate his not-full-self-driving system. Whereas Europe doesn't kowtow to his whims. We'll see what happens in 2029 with a new administration.

That makes the US approach hard to defend. Tesla’s argument for relaxing supervision is that FSD is now good enough. But if that were true, it would be showing the RDW data proving looser monitoring is safe, not adding earlier warnings and harsher strikes to get approved. It’s doing the opposite in Europe because it has to, and the opposite of that in the US because it can.

We’ve been saying it for a while: FSD gets more dangerous as it gets better, because people trust it more and watch the road less. The answer is monitoring that tightens as the system improves. Europe is forcing exactly that. In the US, Tesla is loosening it, encouraging illegal phone use from the top, and leaving drivers with 100% of the liability when it goes wrong.

So here’s the question for Tesla. If European owners are getting earlier warnings and instant strikes, why not American owners on the exact same software? Or is NHTSA going to have to force it?

#4410. Kia went from this one quirky EV 40 years ago to an entire electric lineup

The Kia Besta EV hit the roads in 1986 as the brand’s first fully electric vehicle. 40 years later, Kia continues to “lead the pack” with a full lineup of EVs ranging from entry-level cars and SUVs to three-row models, and just about everything in between.

Kia wanted to design a new vehicle for the 1986 Asian Games, which were held in Seoul, South Korea, one that did not emit any toxic fumes in front of runners.

So, it created the Besta EV. The Besta van was initially developed 40 years ago by Kia’s Central Research Institute as the successor to the popular Bongo van, which is still sold in Korea and other markets today.

Unlike the Bongo, it was developed using Kia’s in-house tech rather than sourced from another automaker and rebadged as its own.

Kia swapped the 2.0L four-cylinder diesel engine for a 35 kWh battery and electric motor, which provided a range of more than 26 miles (42 km) on a single charge.

While the Besta EV was never actually sold to the public, it laid the groundwork and offered an early glimpse at Kia’s shift to electrification.

The first mass-produced Korean EV certified for commercial sale was the Kia Pride EV in 1993. In 2011, the Ray EV became Kia’s first series-production electric car.

Kia expanded its electrification ambitions to Europe and the UK in 2014 with the first-generation Soul EV, the beloved boxy, funky crossover that was discontinued after the 2025 model year.

The Korean automaker has come a long way since the Besta EV, with a full lineup of electric vehicles ranging from compact cars to mid-size and three-row SUVs, vans, and just about everything in between.

Kia now offers an electric option for nearly everyone with seven-passenger EVs on sale in the UK and Europe, including the EV2, EV3, EV4, EV5, EV6, EV9, and PV5 Passenger van.

With its first software-defined vehicle (SDV) and a new B-segment electric hatchback set to launch by the end of 2027, Kia has no plans to slow down. On top of this, Kia will expand its PBV lineup with the PV7 next year, a larger sibling to the PV5.

Four decades after the Besta EV arrived, Kia said it continues to “lead the pack today” with one of the most diverse all-electric EV lineups of any brand.

Through October, Kia has sold over 135,000 EVs in the UK, with fully electric vehicles now accounting for over 37% of total sales.

Thanks to its new EV lineup, Kia became “Europe’s fastest-growing top 10 passenger-car brand.” According to the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association, Kia registered 377,078 vehicles between January and August 2026, up 9% compared to the same period last year.

Sjoerd Knipping, Chief Operating Officer of Kia Europe, said the growth is thanks to having “one of the broadest and most advanced electrified line-ups in Europe.”

In the US, Kia launched the compact EV3 (check out our review of it) this year, starting at just $29,890. It joins the EV6, EV9, and Niro EV in Kia’s US electric vehicle lineup.

#4409. Nearly 1 In 5 Tesla Model Ys Failed Their First German Inspection

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Ask a used Tesla buyer what they’d like checked first, and I’m pretty sure the battery would come up pretty quickly. After reading what German inspectors found underneath some surprisingly young Model Ys, I’d want to know how the suspension was holding up, too.

Germany’s TÜV analyzed 9.7 million mandatory roadworthiness inspections carried out between July 2025 and June 2026. The most revealing comparison was among cars coming in for their first check, at around three years old. EVs won three of the six vehicle classes, but they also occupied the bottom three spots in the overall ranking.

The Model Y finished last out of 109 models for the second year running. Inspectors found major defects on 18.5% of the Model Ys they checked, up from 17.3% a year earlier and nearly triple the 6.4% average for cars that age. No model in that age group recorded a worse result since the 2015 report. Meanwhile, just 3% of Mazda MX-30 EVs failed, good enough for third overall behind the Mazda CX-60 and Mercedes-Benz GLA.

For the Model Y, inspectors flagged worn suspension joints 24 times as often as they did on comparable cars. They also found defective brake discs on 3.4% of Model Ys, against a 1% average for the age group. Front lighting drew more complaints than usual, too.

Tesla Model Ys covered more miles than average, though. By the time they showed up for inspection, the Model Ys had traveled an average of 36,000 miles (58,000 kilometers). The average car in the group had driven 29,200 miles (47,000 km), and the average MX-30 had covered only 16,200 miles (26,000 km). Those Teslas had driven more than twice as far as the Mazdas in roughly the same amount of time.

The MG4 is the first car from a Chinese automaker to appear in the report, and it finished second from the bottom, with a 16% failure rate despite averaging only 23,000 miles (37,000 km). Inspectors flagged brake discs on 10.3% of MG4s, about ten times the average. Suspension defects were also unusually common. Just ahead of the MG was Tesla’s Model 3, with a 12.5% failure rate at an average of 34,200 miles (55,000 km).

The Model Y’s poor performance in Germany runs counter to its reputation for reliability. American buyers may remember that Consumer Reports ranked the Model Y as its most reliable new EV, though that’s based on owners reporting the problems they’d encountered.

Technical inspections, on the other hand, may find play in a suspension joint that the driver hasn’t noticed. There’s also a difference between buying new and buying used, even in Consumer Reports’ own data. Tesla finished last as a brand in its separate survey of five- to ten-year-old cars, which is perhaps more telling.

The German results apply to the Model Y that preceded the Juniper refresh. When I drove the updated Model Y, the softer suspension and new frequency-selective dampers made it noticeably more comfortable. Whether this softer suspension setup holds up better is something we’ll learn as those cars cover more miles.

#4407. Volkwagen’s ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept Sends 362 All-Electric Horsepower to the Front Wheels

It’s not necessarily heading to production, but it sure suggests good things about VW’s EV GTI plans.

Volkswagen’s EV push in America has skewed practical, for the most part. The ID.4 was a generic crossover, so close to an electric take on the Tiguan that VW is actually rebranding it as the ID. Tiguan. And the ID. Buzz, whimsical styling aside, is an electric van—a very expensive electric van. But VW has not abandoned its small, fun hatchback roots in Europe, and the German brand is continuing the celebration of the 50th anniversary of its GTI sub-brand with an EV: the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept, which it will debut at the Essen Motorshow later this month.

The ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept is an all-electric, track-ready, front-wheel drive hot hatch. VW shoehorned an electric drive system intended for larger RWD vehicles into the sub-compact ID. Polo GTI; that gives the concept outputs of 362 horsepower (up to 389 hp in short bursts) and 406 pound-feet of torque, a massive increase from the 223 hp and 214 lb-ft in the standard model.

The ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept can hit a top speed of 149 mph, and it can accelerate from 0-60 mph in 4.7 seconds—quicker than a Golf GTI but not quite as quick as a gas-powered Golf R—with the launch control engaged.

This VW’s body is heavily modified from the standard model, as well. It features a two-door layout instead of four, flared fenders, and an enormous front splitter, diffuser, and rear wing. VW also stripped out the interior for track work by deleting the rear seat and cargo area. The two front seats are Recaro racing bucket seats with five-point harnesses, and the interior also has an integrated Tornado Red roll bar.

Sadly, this is just a concept for now. Volkswagen has not committed to building an ID. Polo GTI Clubsport, and even if the brand did, it would be unlikely to be offered in the American market. VW did reveal a very cool ID. GTI concept back in 2023, which it has claimed will be more fun than the combustion-powered GTIs. And Volkswagen, pointedly, has not ruled out bringing that car to America—though getting the pricing and timing right in the U.S., with an unstable tariff situation and variable EV incentive climate, may prove tricky.

#4405. Americans Bought More Used EVs In October. Fewer Of Them Were Teslas

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

September was a good month to be selling a used Tesla Model Y. Sales jumped nearly 14% from August, and the Ford Mustang Mach-E did even better. The Chevrolet Equinox EV beat both, though, with a nearly 42% increase. A month later, only one of those three electric crossovers was still gaining buyers: the Chevy.

Americans bought an estimated 48,678 used EVs in October, according to the latest EV Market Monitor from Cox Automotive. That’s up 4.7% from September and 73.2% year over year. Used Tesla sales, meanwhile, fell 5.4% from September, with the Model 3, Model Y, and Model X losing ground.

Cox says used EV sales rose 4.7% from September to October. However, its September report put sales at 47,862 vehicles. October’s total of 48,678 is 816 higher, which is a 1.7% gain; Cox doesn’t explain the discrepancy.

Tesla still dominated the used EV scene, though. The change was one spot down, with Chevrolet moving ahead of Ford into second place. Hyundai and BMW rounded out the top five. The Equinox EV and Blazer EV added to their September gains, while the Kia EV6, Nissan Leaf and Volkswagen ID.4 also found more buyers than in the previous month.

Cox says this is because a growing supply of cars coming off lease is giving shoppers more choices across brands and price points.

That 73% jump over last year deserves a little context. October 2025 was the first full month after the federal EV tax credit ended and Americans bought about 30,000 used EVs. In March, sales hit a record of nearly 43,000. EVs made up 3.3% of U.S. used car sales in October, matching September’s record and up from 2% a year earlier.

For used EV shoppers, the more useful number might be $36,582. That was the average asking price for a used EV in October, down from $36,767 in September and 1.9% below a year earlier. The Equinox EV, ID.4, Mach-E and Nissan Ariya all got cheaper.

Used Teslas didn’t for a second consecutive month, rising 1.8% to an average of $34,109. Even after that increase, the average used Tesla was listed for about $2,500 less than the average used EV.

Used EVs still carried a $2,236 premium over gas cars and hybrids, up slightly from $2,137 in September. Dealers had 38 days’ worth of used EVs on hand at October’s sales pace, versus 47 days for gas cars and hybrids.

At October’s sales pace, traditional dealers had enough used Teslas to last 32 days, the shortest supply of any major brand Cox tracked. Cox’s count leaves out Tesla’s own stores. Another study looked at how long each used EV spent on dealer lots in September. The Audi Q4 E-Tron Sportback sold the fastest, and no Tesla made the top ten.

Over on the new-car side, Americans bought 83,262 EVs in October, down 3.9% from September but up 3% from a year earlier, marking the first year-over-year gain of 2026. EVs’ share of new sales slipped from 6.5% in September to 6.2% last month. The average buyer paid $56,221 for a new EV, even with incentives averaging $6,375 per vehicle. Dealers had 85 days’ supply of new EVs, more than double their used inventory.

October wasn’t all bad for Tesla. While sales of second-hand Model Ys fell, Americans bought 36,366 brand-new examples, up 9.4% from September. It accounted for nearly 44% of all new EVs sold in the country.

#4404. California Bans Waymo from Highways, Citing Recent Safety Issues

California has banned Waymo self-driving vehicles from state highways until the company fixes safety concerns related to construction zones and police activity.

California is tightening its restrictions on Waymo’s services. The DMV modified Waymo’s permit last week to ban the driverless vehicles from highways following several examples of the vehicles trying to enter hazardous situations.

The DMV specifically cited two incidents that happened earlier this month. On November 5, three Waymos reportedly drove into a construction zone. The next day, a Waymo vehicle tried to pass California Highway Patrol vehicles that were performing a traffic break. California officials called these vehicles an “imminent hazard to public safety” as long as they continue to ignore road hazards.

See all results for used cars for sale near 07011

This isn’t the first time Waymo has had to pause its highway driving program. In May 2026, the company paused freeway operations to improve vehicle responses in construction zones after similar safety concerns arose.

However, it seems it’s back to the drawing board on construction zone safety. As a result, Waymo is proactively taking all of its vehicles off the freeway until it can develop a solution. The company currently operates in 15 cities, but highway driving was only available in Phoenix, Miami, Austin, Los Angeles County, and the San Francisco Bay Area.

It’s unclear how long the driverless vehicles will stay off the highway. California’s DMV restriction only applies within the state, meaning Waymo could put its vehicles back on the highway in other states before the California ban, which has no distinct end date, is lifted.

State officials say they’ll need solid proof that Waymo vehicles can effectively detect and avoid highway hazards, including construction zones and police activity, before reinstating Waymo’s original license. A Waymo spokesperson told the Associated Press that the company will test highway driving with trained specialists behind the wheel to develop a fix for the safety issues as soon as possible. The autonomous vehicles will continue to operate as usual on non-highway streets.

#4403. IONNA enables Plug & Charge for Tesla, opens 22 bay site in Westminster, CA

IONNA, the DC charging operator backed by several major OEMs, has opened its largest DC charging site yet, with 22 bays of 400kW charging in Westminster, California.

Alongside the opening, IONNA is also enabling Plug & Charge operation for Tesla EVs, with Stellantis EVs “coming soon.”

IONNA is a rapidly expanding DC charging network which is garnering good reviews from EV drivers, with clean, fast and easy to use charging stations (which it calls “Rechargeries”).

But until now, we haven’t had all that many chargers in the LA area. There are a couple in South OC and the Inland Empire, but nothing closer to the population center of the metro area (though more are opening soon).

That changes now with IONNA’s new flagship charging station in Westminster. It features 12 CCS connectors and 10 NACS ports, so you can charge just about any EV (no Chademo, nor can my AC-only Tesla Roadster charge here… ho hum).

In addition to 22 chargers with peak 400kW capacity, the site features indoor and outdoor lounge space, restrooms, and other amenities like an In N Out and a taco shop across the street. (Not quite as full-featured as my favorite charging station, Rove, but IONNA has a much larger national footprint, and does have faster chargers)

There’s also a small, convenience-store-like area that uses Amazon’s “just walk out” technology. You swipe a card to unlock the room, pick up any items you want, and just walk out. The many cameras on the ceiling track you (and whoever came in with you) and what you’re picking up, then charge your card for the items you took with you.

The store has snacks and drinks, though no ice cream, which is the main thing I’m looking for on a roadtrip stop… IONNA may convert one of the fridges to a freezer in the future, depending on how things go.

And, importantly, the site has trash cans and window wipers – just what you need on a roadtrip stop.

Speaking of roadtrips, the charger opening caps off a cross-country roadtrip by IONNA personnel, who set out in several cars from various parts of the country, all convening on the new Rechargery in Westminster.

Over 20 EVs joined the roadtrip and drove over 40,000 combined miles on their trip to Westminster. The teams charged at approximately 30% of the company’s charging sites, showing just how easy it is to do roadtrips in an EV.

The Rechargery opens tomorrow in Westminster, at 6260 Westminster Blvd, just off the 405 freeway. Look for the big sign. For the first weeks, you can charge at a promotional rate of $0.20/kWh. Afterwards, IONNA will charge its standard rate of $0.39/kWh.

Perhaps more importantly than a new charger opening, though, is IONNA’s announcement today that Teslas can now use its network with Plug & Charge functionality (well, technically Autocharge, which is basically the same thing).

Window wipers and fluid are an underrated missing feature at EV stations, hope to see more of this.

What this means is that you can link your car and credit card ahead of time (via the Presto charging app), then simply plug in at any IONNA station and start charging, without having to tap or swipe or open an app. This is similar to the experience Teslas have always had on Superchargers, so should be familiar to Tesla owners.

The functionality is rolled out across all of IONNA’s network, starting today. So you should be able to test it out on your Tesla vehicle. IONNA already supports Plug & Charge for BMW, GM, Hyundai, Kia, Mercedes-Benz, Toyota, Rivian, Ford, Porsche and Volvo EVs.

Further, IONNA says support is “coming soon” for Stellantis EVs (Jeep, Dodge, Ram, Fiat), stating that those cars will be able to Plug & Charge on its network in December. It now supports Autocharge for about two thirds of the EVs on American roads.

#4401. This Hedley Studios Porsche 550 J Is A Shrunken Electric Replica Track Toy

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

This is adorable and I want one. Hedley Studios in the UK just came out with a replica Porsche 550 Spyder, which itself isn't a unique idea. There have been Volkswagen-powered 550 Spyder replicas for decades. What sets this one apart are two things: one is that it's only 80% scale, so it's a little fella, and the other is that it's electric. It's called the Porsche 550 J (for Junior) it looks like a blast.

I can't tell if the 550 J is a track toy or just a toy, but either way it looks like fun. At 80% scale, it looks positively bite-sized next to the real one, which was already one of the smallest production road cars you'll ever see. So it's tiny. So much so, in fact, that I struggle to see how two adults can actually fit in its two seats side-by-side. And, as you'd imagine with such a tiny footprint, the 550 J isn't road legal and is only meant for private roads and race track.

Like a real 550 Spyder, all of the 550 J's weight is behind the driver. Two 1.8 kWh battery packs provide the juice at 48 volts, while a single 11 horsepower electric motor drives the rear wheels. It only weighs 728 pounds, so that power should be enough to have some fun with. Add two passengers, though, and its weight can pretty easily pass the half-ton mark. At that point, 11 horses isn't much. However, there is an optional RS pack that bumps it to 21 horsepower. Top speed also jumps from 40 mph to 50 mph.

The RS Pack also adds two more of those 1.8 kWh battery packs, though, which adds another 44 pounds. That weight penalty might be worth it for the range, though. The standard 550 J only has 30 miles of range, while the RS has 50. That isn't a lot but it's enough for a track day. Plus, with such small batteries, the 550 J will charge up quickly. Lap the track a bunch of times, plug it in and have some lunch, and get back to it.

Track days should be fun, too. Bilstein dampers with Eibach springs handle suspension duty, while Brembo brakes do the stopping. The RS model gets Bilstein adjustable coilovers and drilled brake rotors, too. So despite having Power Wheels-levels of horsepower, it has genuine track car handling bits.

Hedley has done an admirable job of making the 550 J look like a real 550 Spyder that was hit with a shrink ray. It's smaller, sure, but you wouldn't know it from photos. Everything about it looks spot on, from every exterior detail of its carbon fiber body, to the interior switchgear, and even the fuel filler cap. It's a very impressive recreation and one that will look fantastic in owners' garages. Hedley claims it worked closely with the Porsche Museum to get all the details right and it shows.

Only 250 of these will be made, and they'll cost £69,500 ($91,406) each. So it isn't cheap, especially for something that isn't road legal. However, for folks who can afford to spend that kind of cash on a track day toy, this seems like a really fun way to do it.

#4397. Genesis Is Finally Getting Into The U.S. Hybrid Market

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Hyundai and Kia have some of the strongest hybrid lineups on the market. Why did it take so long for Genesis to get there?

Hyundai and Kia hybrids are printing money. Hybrids now account for 29% of all Hyundai sales, a proportion that has grown rapidly over the last few years. But Genesis has so far been left out of the hybrid sales bonanza. No longer. Genesis revealed the G80 and GV80 hybrids on Wednesday, finally entering the fast-growing market for premium hybrids.

The G80 and GV80 are the Genesis brand’s mid-size sedan and SUV, respectively. The G80 competes against cars like the BMW 5 Series and Mercedes E-Class and was—until recently—offered with a fully electric powertrain. That was canned after slow sales, and the GV80 SUV has always been internal-combustion only.

Both models come standard with a 2.5-liter turbocharged gas engine and offer twin-turbo V-6 engines as performance upgrades. The new hybrid system will slot between these two powertrains. It adds a parallel hybrid setup to the 2.5-liter turbocharged powertrain, delivering a combined total of 347 horsepower. The top-trim V6 produces 375 hp, for reference.

Genesis says the GV80 Hybrid is 24% more efficient than the four-cylinder gas model. For that G80 Hybrid, that number is 30%. Final fuel economy ratings are still to come, but that’s a sizable improvement given the extra power it comes with. And like their gas-powered siblings, all G80s and GV80s come with all-wheel-drive.

All G80 and GV80 Hybrids come standard with all-wheel drive.

Kind of. The 2.5T turbo-hybrid combo is used in other Hyundai products like the Palisade Hybrid, but it is among the newest, most sophisticated powerplants in the company’s stable. But the G80 and GV80 do get some Genesis-exclusive hardware. The Genesis hybrids are the first Hyundai Motor Group (HMG) hybrids to feature liquid-cooled batteries. The vast majority of traditional hybrids use small batteries that are passively air-cooled, but as we know from larger EV batteries, active cooling systems are great for long-term stability. Genesis says the cooling system also allows it to take advantage of more of the battery’s energy.

Fundamentally, though, the powertrain should feel similar to existing Hyundai and Kia hybrids. Unlike Honda and Toyota hybrids, HMG hybrids still use traditional transmissions rather than e-CVTs. The G80 and GV80 use a seven-speed automatic, rather than the eight-speed auto that’s employed on the gas models.

The new models offer a “Stay” mode that allows you to run the HVAC and radio for extended periods without firing the gas engine, too, and an EV mode for a limited amount of engine-off cruising.

If you want something that’s more similar to an EV driving experience, Genesis already makes two smaller electric SUVs, the GV60 and Electrified GV70. A third one, the stunning GV90, is coming soon.

But if you want something like a plug-in hybrid, you’ll have to wait for the company’s extended-range electric vehicles (EREVs). EREVs—which use gasoline engines purely as generators, with no direct mechanical between the engine and wheels—are coming in 2027, Genesis confirmed at the debut event. The company says they will offer over 640 miles of combined range. EREV fans will have to wait for further details.

The rear seat of the top-trim Genesis G80 Hybrid.

But if you’re a pure hybrid fan, Genesis finally has a couple of real options. Pricing, trim details, and on-sale dates are still to come. Expect to hear more details next year.

#4396. Electric Vehicles Now Make Up Nearly 1/3rd of Global New Car Sales: Study

The conversion of the automotive industry over to electric vehicles, sold as a foregone conclusion by many car brands in the early 2020s, may have largely stalled out in America, but the picture is far different globally. According to data from the Commonwealth Bank of Australia, EVs now account for 31 percent of all passenger vehicle sales.

And the global increase came despite falling sales in China. The major driver of electric vehicle sales has been Europe; European EV sales have risen 37 percent year over year so far in 2026, climbing to 43 percent of the new vehicle sales market. CommBank data also showed substantial growth rates in countries such as Brazil (EV sales up 164 percent, to a 13 percent market share) and India (EV sales up 76 percent, to a 9 percent market share). Even in Japan, where manufacturers have been notably EV-reticent, sales jumped 80 percent year-over-year to 5 percent of the market.

Meanwhile, electric vehicle sales have declined in the United States this year. According to Cox Automotive data, EV sales made up 6.4 percent of the new car market in Q3 of 2026, down from more than 10 percent in Q3 of 2025. Fuel prices have been elevated this year, but that has led Americans to gravitate toward hybrids rather than fully electric vehicles. Total electrified vehicles now account for nearly 25 percent of the American market.

Much of the decline has been a direct result of Trump administration policies. Last year, the U.S. eliminated a $7500 federal tax credit for electric cars, which—due to a commercial vehicle loophole—made them especially cheap for buyers to lease; the 10 percent share of sales in Q3 2025 came from a glut of sales as buyers rushed to take advantage of the tax credits before they expired. Congress is also considering imposing an annual federal tax on electric cars.

The Trump administration has also effectively eliminated enforcement of America’s CAFE standards, which would have effectively forced manufacturers to sell EVs to avoid hefty fines. American laws and tariffs also effectively prohibit importing affordable Chinese-made EVs, which have been a major reason behind the sales increase in Europe.

While there are seemingly unending restomod companies flooding into the scene every day now, Atlanta-based Vintage Modern is among the most established of them. Starting out seven years ago building a truck that looked like a vintage Bronco yet offered proper modern mechanicals underneath, the company has by now produced some 500 cars and delivered them to celebrities from Mark Wahlberg to LeBron James. Now, it’s expanding its range.

Speaking of celebrities, Vintage Modern’s new Mustang-based Fastback is clearly based on a certain 2000s movie star. The hero car from the Nicolas Cage movie Gone in 60 Seconds, a Chip Foose–customized 1967 Mustang GT500, is well known in the enthusiast community as “Eleanor,” the car Cage couldn’t keep his hands off.

See all results for used cars for sale near 94043

To be clear, Vintage Modern isn’t saying its carbon-fiber-bodied creation is a take on the Eleanor Mustang, but there are plenty of similarities up to and including those massive front lower driving lights. However, underneath things aren’t 1967 but 2026 and newer, with the platform of a modern S650-chassis Mustang providing the basis for the build.

Power starts from a standard 5.0-liter V-8 with 486 horsepower, paired with either a six-speed manual or a 10-speed automatic transmission. Overall, though, what you’re paying for with the Vintage Fastback is the build quality that comes with doing this kind of work for some time. Vintage Modern says that each car represents 900 hours of assembly time, with hand-laid carbon-fiber panels and handcrafted assembly.

Spending that kind of money on a Mustang is a certain kind of flex, but the Fastback’s blend of movie star looks and dependable modern underpinnings should be tempting for those with deep pockets and large Instagram followings. Just maybe lock the keys in a safe if you’re having Nic Cage over for lunch.

#4394. The Next Generation Of U.S.-Made EV Batteries Is Getting Closer To Reality

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Silicon anodes could be the next big thing in lithium-ion battery tech. A new deal paves the way for those more advanced batteries to be made in the U.S.

On Wednesday, Sila Nanotechnologies announced a new multi-year offtake agreement with Panasonic. Sila's role is to supply Panasonic with its silicon-carbon anode material, which the battery giant will use in its U.S. plants to build next-generation battery cells.

We've heard a lot about silicon-carbon batteries over the last few months. Mercedes-Benz bought into the idea, Porsche invested in it too. General Motors is going all-in on the tech, the automaker's battery chief, Kurt Kelty, told us earlier this year. So why the big fuss?

Most lithium-ion batteries use graphite on the anode side. Sila's approach uses silicon, which can hold dramatically more lithium. In theory, that means a more energy-dense battery with no additional weight and faster charging speeds. A win all around.

But, there is a trade-off in the material. Silicon has a habit of "swelling" as it charges and ages due to the sheer amount of extra lithium it can absorb compared to graphite. Sila says its Titan Silicon anode solves this problem by reducing overall expansion to something more akin to traditional graphite-based anodes. Its anodes already help power some consumer electronics, like Whoop bands.

The two companies have been working together to commercialize the tech since 2023 when Panasonic first announced plans to procure anode material from Sila. Now, Panasonic plans to procure it at scale.

Sila's facility in Washington was completed in later 2025 with the ability to produce around 2 Gigawatt-hours of battery material. That's enough to manufacture around 26,000 BEV batteries annually, based on a typical EV battery size of 75 kWh. In July, it secured funding to ramp production to up to 250 GWh. If all goes well, Sila says that Panasonic has the option to offtake more than $1 billion in product over time.

Lamborghini has been offering roofless supercars since the targa Silhouette in 1976, but the 2027 Temerario will be the first Lambo to let the sky in via a folding hardtop rather than a traditional soft top or removable roof. Lambo unveiled the new droptop ahead of the Los Angeles auto show, at the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures. It was a fitting setting for a car that’s all about the panoramic view.

There are no powertrain changes for the Temerario Spyder, and that’s fine with us. We’ve had no complaints about its high-revving hybrid 4.0-liter twin-turbo V-8, dual-motor-assisted all-wheel drive, or eight-speed dual-clutch transmission. The Spyder setup makes the same 907 yowling horsepower and 590 pound-feet of torque, only now you’ll be able to hear that flat-plane crank hit its 10,000-rpm redline through the Akrapovič exhaust with no roof to muffle the scream, like you’re riding that torpedo down from the bomb bay.

See all results for new 2027 Lamborghini Temerario for sale near 07011

It has been decades since the move from coupe to convertible has come with serious compromise in rigidity or weight, so we're not expecting the Temerario Spyder to drop much in performance, but it's still reassuring to hear that the Temerario designers didn't just Sawzall the roof off and call it a day. The coupe’s aluminum spaceframe gets additional stiffening elements and reinforced mounting points, especially behind the seats where the folding roof sits when deployed. Lambo says it’s 6 percent stiffer in both static and dynamic torsional rigidity than the Huracan Spyder.

Lamborghini claims the Spyder will make a 0-to-62-mph run in 2.8 seconds, which is one tenth of a second behind its claim for the coupe. Top speed is a match at 213 mph. The Temerario Spyder comes on 20- or 21-inch wheels with a variety of Bridgestone sport, race, and even winter tires. Carbon-ceramic brakes hide behind the wheels with monoblock binders to bring the whole thing to a stop. We, of course, eagerly look forward to testing all this go and whoa for ourselves.

Software and technology will be familiar to drivers of the Temerario coupe, with 13 different variants of engine and motor matchups, from easygoing Città mode up through Strada, Sport, and Corsa to the serious Corsa ESC Off mode. There are also different settings for Recharge, Hybrid, and Performance, as well as a dedicated launch control button.

What is unique to the Spyder is the roof, a fully electric system of 10 actuators for nearly silent operation that takes 17 seconds to go up or down at speeds up to 31 mph. The roof folds vertically, setting into position behind the seats along the spine of the car, which drops the center of gravity and leaves weight distribution basically unchanged, versus a horizontal stowage which would raise the center of gravity and move weight towards the rear wheels. This arrangement keeps the driving dynamics of the Temerario identical whether the roof is up or down.

See all results for new 2027 Lamborghini Temerario for sale near 07011

While performance driving is prioritized, Lamborghini's engineers also worked to make the top-down experience pleasant for passengers as well. The front windscreen has been tweaked for better airflow over the cabin and away from the interior. An adjustable rear window can also be used to customize the amount of ruffling of one’s hairdo. A neck warmer inside the seatbacks blows warm air over shoulders to counteract the chill of a top-down run through the Italian Alps. The Temerario already had a roomier, more cushioned cockpit than the Huracán’s, and the additional aero and climate elements will only add to the drivability.

Like all high-end brands, Lamborghini specializes in customization. The launch edition of the Temerario Spyder will come in glossy robin's-egg Blu Cepheus paint with black and carbon-fiber details. The more performance-focused Alleggerita package will come in a retina-searing Arancio Egon orange with a carbon-fiber roof and black interior. If neither pleases your palate, Lambo will happily work on the palette with you through its Ad Personam program, which offers choices from among 400 different paint shades, special finishes, carbon details, and one-off options, including personalized illuminated doorsills and dash plaques.

Feeling the wind in your hair will cost you $390,900, and orders start today, November 18, with first deliveries expected in spring 2027.

#4391. Toyota expands C-HR EV recall to 19,000 globally

Toyota is recalling 19,000 electric C-HR SUVs globally, with about 10,000 affected in the US.

In September, Toyota issued a safety recall involving certain model-year 2026 C-HR electric SUVs in North America.

Toyota initially said about 10,000 models were involved, but later confirmed the number was 8,521 in a letter to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA).

According to Germany’s federal motor authority, Kraftfahrt-Bundesamt (KBA), the recall has now expanded to 19,000 C-HR vehicles globally. In Germany, the recall impacts 1,096 vehicles and is still under investigation by the KBA.

The issue stems from faulty software programming in the EV-ECU. While it’s intended to limit the battery’s charge level, the software can cause it to overcharge under certain conditions.

Toyota said the issue occurs if the battery is already at a high state of charge and the driver continues using the regenerative braking system.

When this happens, warning lights and a sound will alert the driver, and the electric drive system can shut down, causing the vehicle to lose power while driving.

Following an internal investigation, Toyota said in the NHTSA report that the issue was caused by incorrect software that disrupted the charging-limit function, allowing the battery to overcharge while driving.

The Toyota C-HR vehicles included in the recall were produced between June 17, 2025, and July 9, 2026.

In Europe and other overseas markets, Toyota sells the C-HR EV as the C-HR+ to distinguish it from the gas- or hybrid-powered version.

OTA would be great, but there are some systems that are isolated and can't be updated that way. The EV-ECU is a core function system that is very likely sealed to prevent tampering. They never expected to need to reprogram it. It's like the firmware on your phone.

Owners of affected vehicles in North America can take them to a Toyota dealership, where the battery ECU software will be updated free of charge.

Toyota mailed owner notification letters out on October 18, 2026. Owners can contact Toyota’s customer service at 1-800-331-4331. The recall number is 26TA17.

Other than saying the EV-ECU is being reprogrammed, Toyota has not yet announced next steps for owners of affected vehicles outside North America. The KBA reference number is 17116R.

Check back for more details. The recall only affects the 2026 C-HR. The 2027 Toyota C-HR is also now on sale.

Tesla is now rolling out rides in the Cybercab in Dallas, its second major city after the service launched in Austin in September, the automaker said in a post on X Thursday. The driverless taxi can carry up to two passengers at a time and doesn’t have a steering wheel or pedals. Riders can order a Cybercab using the Tesla Robotaxi app on their smartphones.

The automaker was already serving Dallas with its Model Y robotaxis, but this is the first time the purpose-built Cybercab is joining its fleet there. Tesla’s robotaxi rollout has been heavily concentrated in Texas and Florida, since those two states have fewer regulations, letting Tesla add vehicles and expand its geofenced areas more quickly than in other states.

In addition to Austin and Dallas, Tesla is currently serving riders in Houston, Fort Worth, Tampa, San Antonio, Orlando, and Miami. The service also runs in the San Francisco Bay Area, but those vehicles have drivers supervising them due to California’s rules. The two-door Cybercab is only present in Austin and Dallas, with the rest of the cities getting the Model Y.

CEO Elon Musk has said the company eventually plans to have two million Cybercabs in the U.S. That figure deserves some skepticism, given Tesla’s track record of promising big numbers and failing to deliver them. Tesla also plans to wind down Cybertruck production at Gigafactory Austin next summer to ramp up Cybercab production.

Tesla recently said it’s sending out invites to select customers to purchase the Cybercab for private use, but that news raised more questions than it answered. The car won’t operate without a $299 per month autonomy subscription, and it’s unclear how it will meet the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards. Tesla also plans to roll out a version of the Model Y without a steering wheel and pedals to add to its robotaxi fleet.

#4389. US battery storage just topped 200 GWh – here’s where it is

The US has installed more than 200 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of battery storage, with nearly 50 GWh coming online in the first nine months of 2026 alone.

The US added 48.3 GWh of battery storage through September, up 20% from the same stretch last year, according to the latest report from the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. Q3 was a little slower: The US installed 14.3 GWh in those three months, down 1% year over year.

Texas added 12.3 GWh of grid-scale batteries through September, more than any other state. Arizona came in second at 7.7 GWh, followed by California at 6.8 GWh. And 11 states had already broken their annual storage installation records with three months to go – Colorado, Massachusetts, Utah, Michigan, Georgia, Mississippi, Virginia, Iowa, Montana, Alabama, and Illinois.

Utility-scale batteries did most of the work in Q3, accounting for 12.2 GWh of new capacity. Businesses and industrial sites added another 1.3 GWh, and residential added 746 megawatt-hours (MWh). That was the best Q3 yet for home batteries, though installs through September were still down 12% year over year. Some homeowners moved up their installations last year before the federal residential clean energy tax credit ended.

“States are moving from targets to centralized procurements,” said Pete Tillotson, a senior analyst at Benchmark. In September, New York awarded contracts for eight battery projects that can deliver about 950 megawatts (MW) combined. SEIA and Benchmark now expect 708 GWh of storage across the grid, homes, and businesses by 2030, up 3.7% from their previous forecast.

The US can also make more battery cells here. A Tennessee factory opened in July and an Indiana factory opened in October, bringing US cell manufacturing capacity to 92.4 GWh, up 50%.

Solar and batteries helped bring down average summer wholesale power prices by 42% in Texas’s ERCOT market and 51% in California’s CAISO market between 2021 and 2026, according to SEIA’s inflation-adjusted analysis. When batteries had power to spare during peak hours, grid operators could call on expensive power plants less often.

You wouldn’t know it from looking at the total on residential electric bills. The cost of generating power for households fell in both markets, but the cost of delivering it to homes rose. Overall, residential bills rose 22% at the two California utilities SEIA examined and 3% across its Texas utility sample, driven by higher transmission and distribution costs. California is upgrading its grid to reduce the risk of wildfires. Texas is expanding its grid for rising demand and make it more resilient to storms.

The article is good with the reporting about grid tied storage, but seems to miss the forest for the trees with it comes to pricing. Texas isn't installing more grid tied storage because of altruistic intent.

The storage is being added because they electricity suppliers can use it to make money. They can make money because we have a reasonably well thought out wholesale electrical market AND because that market has purchases large amounts of solar and wind generation.

That combination means that I still pay just $0.01 more per kwh than I did when I moved to this state 20 years ago. I pay 12 cents per kwh and Texas average is between 12 and 15. A functional market is what makes that work.

More than 300 solar and battery storage companies in the US wrote to Congress last week asking it to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. SEIA CEO Tim Pawlenty says the permitting bill would help get projects built faster and ease pressure on power prices. However, many Democrats feel this bill falls short. The Senate voted 70–27 on Monday to end debate on the amendment containing the bill’s text, moving it closer to a final vote.
