#4324. Tiny magnets deep inside the brain could transform Parkinson’s treatment

An international research team has developed a new technique that uses magnetic fields and tiny particles to stimulate regions deep inside the brain, potentially opening the door to a less invasive treatment for Parkinson's disease. In experiments involving mice with Parkinson's-like symptoms, the approach significantly improved movement problems without requiring permanently implanted electrodes.

The technique involves injecting specially designed magnetic nanoplatelets into a targeted area of the brain. When exposed to an external magnetic field, these particles generate tiny forces that activate nearby nerve cells. Unlike conventional brain stimulation treatments, which rely on surgically implanted electrodes, the new approach uses magnetic forces to influence brain activity. The findings, published in Advanced Science, come from researchers at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU), RWTH Aachen, and the Universities of Maastricht (the Netherlands) and Leuven (Belgium).

Why Parkinson's Treatment Often Requires Brain Implants

Parkinson's disease develops as brain cells responsible for producing dopamine gradually break down. Dopamine is a chemical messenger that plays a vital role in controlling movement. As its levels decline, communication within the brain's movement circuits becomes disrupted, contributing to tremors and other motor difficulties.

For some patients, deep brain stimulation can help control these symptoms. This treatment uses a device known as a brain pacemaker, which is implanted beneath the collarbone and connected to electrodes placed deep inside the brain. The electrodes deliver electrical stimulation to a region called the subthalamic nucleus (STN for short), helping to modify abnormal activity in the brain circuits responsible for movement.

Although this treatment can provide substantial relief, it requires a complex surgical procedure and does not work for everyone.

"The procedure is relatively complex, however, and not always successful," explains Prof. Dr. Danijela Gregurec from the Department of Chemistry and Pharmacy at FAU. "This puts many Parkinson's patients off, and not all patients are suitable candidates for one of these pacemakers."

The researchers believe magnetic stimulation could eventually provide another option, allowing doctors to influence the same deep brain structures without leaving electrodes permanently implanted.

How Tiny Magnetic Particles Stimulate Brain Cells

The new technology takes advantage of the ability of certain nerve cells to detect physical pressure and mechanical forces.

"We use magnetic nanoparticles that we implant in the brain," Gregurec explains. "They have a special shape and a magnetic structure. They were developed in order to transform magnetic fields into tiny mechanical forces."

Rather than sending electrical pulses directly into the brain, the technique uses these particles to produce extremely small physical movements when a magnetic field is applied.

"The traditional method establishes an electrical connection to the brain," she says. "In contrast, we use the neurons' natural mechanosensors to influence regions deep within the brain."

The process works by gently changing the shape of nearby nerve cell membranes. Imagine pressing a finger against an inflated balloon and creating a small indentation in its surface. The magnetic particles produce a similar effect on a microscopic scale.

This slight deformation opens specialized channels in the cell membrane that respond to mechanical pressure. Once opened, these channels allow electrically charged particles called ions to enter the nerve cells, changing their electrical activity and providing a way to stimulate the targeted brain circuits.

Magnetic Brain Stimulation Improves Movement in Mice

To investigate whether the technology could relieve Parkinson's symptoms, the international research team conducted experiments using mice with damage to the same types of dopamine-producing nerve cells affected by the disease in humans. This damage caused movement difficulties resembling those seen in Parkinson's patients.

"Together with our partners from Maastricht, we injected magnetic nanoparticles developed here at FAU into the animals' subthalamic nucleus," Gregurec explains. "That is the very region in the brain that is also an important target for conventional deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease."

The researchers used precise stereotactic injection techniques to deliver the particles to the intended location. These methods rely on carefully calculated three-dimensional coordinates to guide instruments into specific brain structures. Accurate placement was particularly important because the treatment needed to affect the correct neural circuits involved in movement.

After the particles were positioned, the researchers applied an external magnetic field. The results were encouraging: the mice showed significant improvements in their movement deficits.

"The effect is roughly equivalent to what we would have expected after implanting a brain pacemaker," says Gregurec.

The findings suggest that magnetic nanoparticles could provide a different way to achieve some of the benefits of conventional deep brain stimulation, without the need for permanently implanted electrodes.

Could Future Parkinson's Treatments Use Magnetic Headbands?

Another encouraging finding involved how the brain responded to the implanted particles over time. The magnetic nanoparticles remained in place throughout an observation period lasting several months, and the researchers found no signs of inflammation. This suggests that the particles were well tolerated during the experiments.

However, delivering the particles still required an injection directly into the brain. Gregurec and her colleagues are now investigating ways to make the procedure even less invasive.

One possibility is to develop particles that could be injected into the bloodstream and then travel into the brain by crossing the blood-brain barrier. This protective boundary normally prevents many substances circulating in the blood from entering brain tissue. Finding a way to deliver the particles across it could eliminate the need for direct brain injections.

The researchers are also exploring compact wearable devices capable of generating the magnetic fields needed for stimulation. One possibility is a headband that patients could put on themselves, potentially making treatment more convenient and adjustable.

These ideas remain at an early stage, and the researchers expect that several more years of development will be needed before the technology could be considered for clinical use.

"Nevertheless, we are convinced that the new method has enormous potential," Gregurec states. "It is not only considerably simpler and cheaper than a conventional brain pacemaker, it is probably also more flexible. Adjusting the parameters of the magnetic field would allow us to control the nanoparticles more accurately."

Beyond its potential medical applications, the technology could also become a valuable scientific tool. By allowing researchers to stimulate nerve cells through carefully controlled mechanical forces, it offers a new way to explore how physical changes at the cellular level influence brain activity.

Although the treatment has so far been demonstrated only in animals, its ability to improve movement without permanently implanted electrodes represents a promising step toward new approaches to Parkinson's disease and brain stimulation.

#4322. When the Work Gets Heavy, Do Your Tires Hold Up? Cooper’s New Discoverer® HT Is Built to Carry the Weight

Evolved from severe-duty all-terrain designs and backed by an up to 70,000-mile Limited Treadwear Warranty, this highway tire pairs interlocking 3D tread sipes with rigid construction to keep your truck or SUV composed on high-mileage trips.

For enthusiasts, tire shopping is an upgrade, not a chore. While the casual driver might treat new tires like regular maintenance, anyone who cares about vehicle dynamics knows that what meets the road defines how a truck or SUV rides, tracks, and stops. It is the single most transformative upgrade you can make to your vehicle. For more than 110 years, Cooper tires have catered to drivers who look past the showroom floor and seek out products that overdeliver on performance, capability, and long-term durability.

And that level of purpose-built engineering is more vital than ever. As vehicles grow heavier and more capable, tires need to do more than simply roll down an interstate. They have to withstand heavy payload demands, sudden weather changes, and unpredictable pavement. Cooper tires are built to that benchmark. Rooted in American engineering and real-world development, Cooper tires are built to an uncompromising standard that live up to their promises. From the rock-crawling STT Pro to the severe-snow-designated Stronghold AT, the Discoverer® family has earned its reputation through real-world testing from Alaskan ice to jagged mountain trails.

The new Cooper Discoverer® HT adapts that rugged all-terrain lineage for long-distance highway cruising, matching heavy-duty capability with quiet, refined composure. While it retains the structural durability to wander down a gravel trail with a trailer in tow, its core mission is maximizing comfort and control across hundreds of miles of open road.

Where many highway tires trade load capability for a soft ride, the Discoverer® HT is engineered to handle both. Straight, reinforced sidewalls provide the structural foundation needed to maintain an optimal contact patch under load. Whether the vehicle is running light or carrying family, gear, and tongue weight, the tire resists deformation, ensuring consistent steering response and predictable roadholding grip in any condition. It’s engineered for drivers whose tires have to hold their own—providing a dependable, hard-working partner that won’t fold when the truck or SUV is pushed to its limit.

Cooper tires also tackle truck and SUV tire performance, with advanced features. Its proprietary 3-D Micro-Gauge Siping incorporates interlocking zig-zag sipes inside the tread blocks. Under heavy braking, sharp turns, or loaded acceleration, these interlocking sipes lock together to stiffen the tread block, to help support responsiveness. Crucially, these sipes run deep into the tread rubber, ensuring that gripping edges are still present to help with traction. That structural integrity backs up an exceptional UTQG treadwear rating of 720 and a 70,000-mile limited treadwear warranty on passenger fitments.

This is the tire for drivers who expect their trucks or suvs to show up for the long haul. Whether that means towing a camper into the backcountry, handling moving-day payloads, or eating up cross-country interstate miles in quiet comfort, the mission remains the same: a single set of tires that balances real-world traction, refined manners, and hard-working capability.

To fit that wide spectrum of work, Cooper offers the Discoverer® HT across 19 passenger sizes covering 16- to 22-inch wheels (with section widths from 245 to 285 mm), alongside 16 light-truck (LT) options engineered with deeper tread grooves and higher load ratings. Backed by a 45-day satisfaction guarantee and over a century of research and development, the Discoverer® HT delivers what Cooper has always stood for: the quiet confidence that the job was done right.

Find out more about the Cooper Discoverer® HT on Coopertire.com or visit your local tire shop retailer.

#4321. Battlefield 6 gets a new map today alongside major changes to controller aim assist, and even more weapon dispersion tweaks

Right on schedule, the latest Battlefield 6 patch has arrived to kick off the next stage of Season 1.

Battlefield 6’s first season has entered its second phase. The game received a major update earlier today, version 1.1.2.0, which delivers a host of changes to the game, many of which have been expected.

The update, of course, also adds new content to the game in the form of the map Eastwood, as well as new hardware and fresh features for the multiplayer sandbox.

We’ve known about the new content side of today’s patch for quite some time. The update kicks off the California Resistance stage of Season 1, which is the second of three. The new Eastwood map takes place in California, and it’s a map cut from the larger Battlefield Redsec battle royale map of Fort Lyndon.

There’s a new limited-time mode called Sabotage - a tactical, 8v8 mode where two teams attempt to destroy as many bomb sites as possible. The other big new feature that arrives today is Battle Pickups.

These are powerful weapons which can be found in specific game modes (and in Portal), scattered around the map for players to pick up and use. They have limited ammo that cannot be replenished, and deliver incredible firepower.

Redsec players have a new Gauntlet mission to look forward to that joins the existing modes. It’s called Rodeo and it involves a lot of vehicular action. Finally, everyone gets to unlock two new weapons: the the DB-12 shotgun, and the M327 Trait revolver sidearm. There’s also a new angled grip attachment.

The fixes and tweaks side of the patch is arguably the more interesting. Controller aim assist has received a big overhaul that essentially resets everything to open beta settings. The goal is to make infantry targeting more consistent.

Controller players actually get the bulk of the changes in this update, which also improves input latency and stick response. Several issues that reset aim assist values, or make it behave erratically, have been addressed.

The conversation around weapon bloom/spread doesn’t look like it’s ever going to end, because Battlefield Studios is yet again tuning gunplay to fix unintended dispersion behaviour, and decrease its intensity across the board.

Certain Challenges have had their description rewritten so their requirements can be better understood. Beyond that, you can expect several deployables to behave much more consistently, including several bug fixes there, too.

Head to the official blog for the full rundown of patch 1.1.2.0.

#4318. Ozempic and Mounjaro may have a surprising effect on your brain

Popular medications used to treat obesity and type 2 diabetes, including semaglutide and tirzepatide, may have effects that extend beyond weight loss and blood sugar control. These drugs also influence biological processes involved in brain function, raising questions about whether they could help preserve memory and thinking abilities.

To examine this possibility, researchers from the University of Gothenburg and the University of Copenhagen reviewed the existing scientific evidence at the invitation of the journal Science.

Studies involving animals suggest that GLP-1 medications can influence learning and memory. However, research involving humans has produced less consistent findings. Analyses of patient health records have found an association between GLP-1 treatment and a reduced risk of dementia among people with type 2 diabetes. These observational findings are encouraging, but they cannot determine whether the medications themselves are responsible for the lower risk.

More definitive results have also raised questions. In Novo Nordisk's EVOKE and EVOKE+ clinical trials, semaglutide failed to slow the progression of early Alzheimer's disease. Although the treatment affected several biological markers associated with Alzheimer's, those changes did not translate into a measurable slowing of the disease.

Why Weight Loss Drugs May Still Benefit the Brain

Despite the disappointing Alzheimer's results, researchers believe GLP-1 medications could still offer cognitive benefits to certain groups of patients.

People living with obesity or type 2 diabetes sometimes experience difficulties with attention, planning, and the speed at which they process information. These cognitive problems are often associated with metabolic health and blood vessel function, suggesting they may respond differently to treatment than the changes caused by Alzheimer's disease.

Improving blood sugar regulation, metabolism, or vascular health could potentially help preserve cognitive abilities, even if the same medications cannot slow an established neurodegenerative disease.

Stina Börchers, the review's first author and a researcher affiliated with both the University of Gothenburg and the University of Copenhagen, emphasizes the need to determine whether starting treatment earlier could make a difference.

"We need to find out whether these treatments can help people with obesity or diabetes preserve their cognitive abilities, particularly if treatment begins before cognitive problems become established. It is also important to identify which patients might benefit," says Stina Börchers.

Unlocking New Treatments to Protect Memory

A central unanswered question is how GLP-1 medications might influence the brain. Their potential cognitive effects could result from improvements in metabolic health, direct actions within the brain, or a combination of both.

Understanding these mechanisms could help researchers identify which patients are most likely to benefit and potentially lead to medications designed specifically to support memory and other thinking abilities.

Christoffer Clemmensen, the review's senior author and a research group leader at the University of Copenhagen, sees an opportunity to use increasingly advanced obesity treatments to explore the connection between metabolism and the brain.

"Obesity medicines are becoming increasingly sophisticated, offering new opportunities to understand how metabolic regulation influences brain function. By disentangling the direct and indirect effects of these drugs on the brain, we may ultimately be able to develop treatments specifically aimed at preserving cognitive function," says Christoffer Clemmensen.

The researchers are calling for clinical trials that evaluate memory, attention, and other cognitive abilities beginning when patients first start treatment. Following these changes over time could help establish whether GLP-1 drugs genuinely protect brain function and clarify who might benefit most.

They also stress that treatment is not without potential drawbacks, particularly for older adults and people who are physically frail. Rapid weight loss can lead to a reduction in muscle mass, which may weaken physical function and offset some of the possible benefits.

Careful monitoring will therefore be essential as researchers investigate whether today's weight loss and diabetes medications could eventually provide new ways to protect the brain.

#4317. Battlefield 6 is getting a free trial next week with... a questionable selection of maps, but at least the modes are good

If Redsec got you hooked on Battlefield gameplay but you never experienced traditional multiplayer in Battlefield 6, there's an upcoming moment you might want to pay attention to.

Presumably as a way of marching ever forward towards its (alleged) 100 million player goal for Battlefield 6, EA has announced that the multiplayer shooter will be getting its first free trial later this month.

This is, of course, specifically for players to sample the core, paid component of the game, as the recently launched Redsec remains free-to-play. Redsec, however, offers modes like battle royale and Gauntlet, which aren’t quite the traditional Battlefield experience.

The Battlefield 6 trial arrives next Tuesday, November 25. It will run for one week, ending the following Tuesday, December 2. The trial will be available on all platforms, but won’t include all content from the full game.

Instead, players will have access to three of the game’s maps and five of its modes. Siege of Cairo will be there alongside Season 1’s two new maps: Eastwood, and Blackwell Fields. It’s not the strongest line-up of maps, considering Eastwood is already cut from the larger Fort Lyndon battle royale map that Redsec players should be quite familiar with, but it’s something.

As for modes, you can pick from Conquest, Breakthrough, Sabotage, and Team Deathmatch. Battlefield Studios didn’t say what the fifth mode is going to be, but a dedicated blog post with more information is set to arrive next week.

Beyond the trial's content itself, the timing is certainly great. Battlefield 6 just received one of its biggest patches, kicking off the second phase of its first season. So far this season, we’ve seen two new maps, several new weapons - but more importantly, solutions to problems the game’s had since launch, as well as fixes to longstanding bugs.

The miserable XP progression Battlefield 6 launched with is far more tolerable. Challenges and Assignments are much easier to understand and actually finish. The often maligned weapon dispersion has been toned down. Some of the wildest vehicle bugs have been fixed. And Portal has a host of experiences that go beyond just bot farms.

In essence, Battlefield 6 feels like its reached its 1.0 status, which makes this a great entry point for new players, even if the trial could've used more of the game's better maps.

According to VanDyke, some of the Rampage’s expected success could come from fleet sales, though the executive doesn’t see corporate sales as a large piece of the pie. “There is a commercial aspect to it,” VanDyke said. “It’s still going to be a vast majority [of sales] retail; it’s not going to be a ProMaster City van or anything, but there absolutely is an upside there.”

The Rampage is set to arrive around the same time as the upcoming mid-size Dakota pickup. According to VanDyke, the smaller Rampage will be focused on affordability and practicality, while the larger Dakota will be able to target buyers who don’t want to deal with a full-size pickup.

“Dakota is going to enable us to do some serious fun things and some things that someone like you would expect the crazy people here to do from a power, performance, trim, variant perspective,” VanDyke said. Exactly how much power and performance Ram is planning is still a mystery, but we like what we’re hearing so far.

#4314. Battlefield 6 streamlines some of the most annoying Challenges yet again, takes out a few of them entirely

The easier and more accessible Battlefield Studios makes those Battlefield 6 Challenges, the better.

The work to continue streamlining Challenges in Battlefield 6 is clearly not done. Having just released a new patch - which already included several updates to Challenges and Assignments - Battlefield Studios has gone in and made even more changes.

This latest round includes far fewer tweaks, but quite surprisingly, it also removes a few of the more annoying ones from the game.

The updated list, which Battlefield shared on Twitter, includes changes to the dreaded Recon 2 headshots beyond 150m Challenge. Now, any headshot beyond 75m will count. Recon Expert 3 is another headshot-themed one that’s been updated, and now requires getting headshot kills beyond 125m, rather than the practically impossible beyond 200m that it required previously.

The Rapid Fire 2 Challenge, which required getting kills beyond 50m with Assault Rifles, has been changed so it now tracks anything beyond 40m. The painful ‘Inflict damage under 15m while hip-firing with Assault Rifles’ has been entirely replaced with one that requires - the far more sensible - inflicting damage while in ADS with Assault Rifles.

A couple of Challenges, such as the one that required suppressing enemies with LMGs, and another that wanted you to deal damage to laser-designated vehicles using lock-on weapons, have both been removed.

The journey to make Challenges and Assignments easier to complete has been a long one. Progression has been one of the key areas of criticism Battlefield 6 received at launch. The issue encompassed more than just slow player and weapon XP earn rates, it also prevented players from accessing new Training Paths for the various classes, and several of the game's weapons.

Battlefield Studios attacked the problem from multiple angles, initially boosting the XP players and their weapons would earn, before later reducing the requirements of the Challenges themselves. The developer continued to streamline those requirements over multiple patches, including majorly overhauling the system earlier this month.

It seems the studio is more confident than ever in the game, as it recently announced that Battlefield 6 will be getting its first free trial next week, offering players who do not own the full game access to iconic modes like Conquest, and Breakthrough - though on an unusual selection of maps.

#4313. This 500 kWh energy storage system runs on retired EV batteries

A retired EV battery can still have years of use left in it when it’s taken off the road. Moment Energy’s new Nova battery storage system puts those packs to work on commercial sites. And when a pack wears out, it can be swapped without pulling out the whole system.

Nova was unveiled at RE+ in Las Vegas this week, and it’s already in production at Megafactory 1, the battery-repurposing plant that Moment Energy opened in the Vancouver area in June.

Each Nova unit delivers 500 kilowatt-hours (kWh) of energy and 200 kilowatts (kW) of power. It has a 2.94 m by 1.80 m (9.7 x 5.9 ft) footprint, and units can be linked together for projects in the tens of megawatt-hours. A site could charge the batteries when electricity is cheaper or when its solar panels are producing more than it needs, then draw on that power when demand spikes or the grid goes down.

Nova can use packs from different EV models, even when those packs have aged at different rates. Moment’s battery management software tracks how each pack is doing. As packs wear out, the company can replace them while leaving the enclosure and concrete pad in place. Moment says its pack replacement service could keep a system in service for more than 20 years.

“We see a future where reengineered EV batteries become essential infrastructure for powering businesses and onshoring manufacturing and supply chains. Nova brings that vision to life, combining safety, engineering, and North American manufacturing to deploy the safest and highest-performance batteries ever made: EV batteries to supercharge our aging grid,” said Edward Chiang, co-founder and CEO of Moment Energy.

Moment Energy says Nova is the first storage system built from retired EV batteries to earn both UL 1973 certification for the batteries and UL 9540 certification for the complete system. It was also tested under UL 9540A, which looks at how a battery fire can spread. The factory itself is certified under UL 1974, which covers how used batteries are assessed and graded for reuse.

That matters for businesses with limited space. Nova is designed to sit outdoors alongside the buildings it serves. It uses liquid cooling, detects smoke, heat, and flammable gases, and is rated to operate from −13F to 122F (−25C to 50C).

Moment Energy also says an independent review found that Nova meets US federal sourcing restrictions tied to the clean electricity investment tax credit. Those rules are one part of determining whether a project qualifies for the credit.

Orders are open, and Moment Energy expects the first units to ship in Q1 2027 for deployments across North America.
